newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FEATURE - Australia's Catholic church in bid to reduce paedophilia.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Australia's Catholic church in bid to reduce paedophilia.

text.p: Australia's Catholic church has for the first time hired a world expert on child sexual abuse to help rid its priesthood of paedophiles, as senior clergy add up the cost of denying their existence for decades.

The church, rocked in recent years by a barrage of complaints and law suits from people abused as children, brought British sex-abuse expert Ray Wyre to Australia this month to teach priests around the country how to identify paedophilia.
Wyre, the founder of an internationally recognised London clinic for sex offenders, comes straight to the point.
"The Catholic church probably has more of a problem than any other organisation because of the autonomy of its employees," he told priests here in the first of a series of training seminars.
Wyre suggests priests should no longer be allowed to be left alone with a child in some circumstances and urges the church to draw up its own definitions of "inappropriate" behaviour.
"You may say that no staff member or priest will take a boy or a girl home after 11 o'clock at night," he said, warning that priests can be especially good at disguising their paedophilia.
"Priests more than any other group are chameleons. They can adapt to their environment and say the right things," he said.

Wyre, who has conducted similar seminars for churches in the United States and Europe, also confronted priests on the issue of celibacy and asked them to acknowledge that the no-sex rule was drawing paedophiles into the priesthood.

"There are some people coming into the church with a belief that celibacy itself will solve a sexual problem," said Wyre, who then played video-taped interviews with former priests treated at the London clinic, run by his Lucy Faithful Foundation.
Wyre uses the tapes to show how uncontrolled sexual fantasies motivate paedophiles and has urged senior clergy here to start quizzing would-be priests on their sexuality.
"I think seminaries and their selection of priests do have to have sex on their agenda," Wyre told the seminar.
In one of the videos, a bespectacled, middle-aged priest from an order that practised ritual flagellation explains the fantasy that led him to abuse children on church retreats.
"I fantasised about nudity and spanking or being spanked," says the priest.

The Catholic church, Australia's biggest, is not the only church dealing with the issue of sexual abuse here. But it has been the focus of a recent storm of fresh claims of sexual assault, against priests and Christian brothers nationwide.

The church faces millions of dollars in compensation claims to the victims of sexual abuse and formally apologised to them all in April, after an official inquiry into police corruption in Sydney stumbled on sex-abuse cases covered up by the church.
The Catholic church in Australia has already taken some of Wyre's advise and is drafting a code of conduct to address issues such as when a priest can be left alone with a child.

Its national professional standards committee is also developing a therapy programme for priests who have abused or who feel they may abuse, said the committee's executive officer, Father David Cappo.
"This is a major public and community issue and we've got to learn quickly how to respond to it," Cappo told Reuters.
But decades of failing to prosecute or even acknowledge sexually abusive priests has left deep scars on their victims.

"I came into this forum with the perfect solution to child sexual abuse -- hang 'em. Hang them from their neck until they're dead," said David, 40, who was sexually abused as a young child by a priest.

"I did not have a childhood, not a childhood as such...The priest insinuated himself into the family. My mother took me to visit him quite frequently. The whole family knew him," David told Reuters. He was invited to attend one of the seminars.
David, who spoke on the condition his full name was not used, was abused for six years from the age of six by a priest in Scotland, before David's family immigrated to Australia.
He says he has spent much of his adult life wrestling with alcohol and drug problems, and suicide.
"You feel incredibly guilty when you think back as an adult as to 'why did I let him do that to me?' It's very confusing and very disturbing," David said.

David kept silent on the abuse for over 30 years, until last December when he and many others began speaking publicly about their abuse. David cannot prosecute because the priest who abused him is dead, but he welcomes the church's recent apology.
"Basically it's the church crucifying itself, and that's maybe what the church has to do. There's no simple solution, but there has to be some way of restoring trust," he said.
"But you never get justice in this situation. Justice does not exist."
